ch13.anchor: forge a spear that will pierce your shield
ch13.note: The image is an old Chinese one, and the modern word for ‘contradiction’ is made of it. In a parable set down by the philosopher Han Fei (third century BCE), a man of Chu hawking arms cried up his shields as so stout that nothing could pierce them, and in the same breath his spears as so sharp that they would pierce anything at all; when a bystander asked what would happen were one of his spears driven against one of his shields, the man had no answer. From his spear (矛, mao) and his shield (盾, dun) comes the word maodun (矛盾), ‘contradiction’ — two claims that cannot both stand. Zhu Ting’s door, and the trap it undid, are the parable made flesh.

ch13.anchor: little fox-spirit can keep you company
ch13.note: A huli jing (狐狸精), literally a ‘fox-spirit,’ is a creature of Chinese folklore: a fox that has cultivated the power to take human shape, most often that of a ravishing woman, and so bewitches men and drains them. In common speech the word is an insult flung at a seductress or a husband-stealer, with no ghostly force left in it — which is all the Boss’s Wife means here in her jealousy of Shangguan Xue’er, and all Hua Manlou means by his quip a little later that a second wife is commonly a ‘little fox-spirit.’ It is a distinct thing from the plain ‘little fox’ (小狐狸) that Lu Xiaofeng and others are called elsewhere, which marks only slyness.

Shangguan Xue’er closes the volume on the very words with which Lu Xiaofeng closed the chapter before — ‘Why is it that when I tell the truth, no one will ever believe me?’ — the liar and the honest man left, each, with the same complaint. Here the source edition prints its end-mark, 《The Legend of Lu Xiaofeng: The Golden Roc Dynasty》 ends, and directs the reader onward: for the tale that follows, see The Legend of Lu Xiaofeng 2: The Embroidery Bandit (《陆小凤传奇2：绗花大盗》). The story of the vanished Shangguan Feiyan, glimpsed here as an old herb-gathering woman, is taken up in that second volume.
